281.name: A Wide Path Through a Patch of Trees
281.description: The path here runs through a small patch of wind-bent trees, every trunk leaning the same way because the weather here only ever comes from one direction. The heads of several red deer lie in the grass at the side of the trail, the remains of a successful hunt and a careless butcher. The cliffs to the east are quite visible now and look rather impressive against the hazy sea sky. Gulls turn above them, and a band of paler rock around the mid-section forms Draken's Belt, a centre of local folklore. The quality of the path is still quite impressive considering it does not appear to be part of the main road. The path continues through the patch of trees to the east.

430.name: The Edge of the Flatlands
430.description: The surroundings on either side of the path are absolutely barren. Nothing is in sight for miles to the north, while far to the south, past the cataract, a forest is visible, but no sign of civilisation other than the road itself. The cliffs are now visible without any obstruction and their true grandeur becomes apparent. They seem to rise forever, as if seeking to join the heavens, and the top of them is not really visible at all: it is shrouded in the sea haar that from a greater distance looked like nothing more than weather. There is nothing on this road to speak of, and it is still disturbingly well maintained. The flatlands continue to the east.

431.name: A Road Through the Flatlands
431.description: The road continues here, running east-west through the vast flatlands. There is no sign of life in the immediate area. It is quite barren, with the only shelter in sight being the forest to the west and the cliffs to the east. Cart tracks pressed into the dried mud provide a hint of usage, but they look at least a few days old and the last rain has begun to take them. Nothing is in sight for miles to the north, while far to the south, past the cataract, a forest is visible, but no sign of civilisation other than the road itself. There is nothing on this road to speak of, and it is still disturbingly well maintained. The flatlands continue to the east.

432.name: A Road Through the Flatlands
432.description: The road continues here, running east-west through the vast flatlands. There is no sign of life in the immediate area. 433.name: Nearing the Cliff Base
433.description: This is the end of the road through the flatlands. Just to the east the base of the cliffs can be seen. Some scrub bushes and a few salt-stunted trees have started to sprout up in the shelter of the cliffs, but nothing substantial. Small tracks in the dust show signs of wildlife, but again nothing of an intelligent nature seems to reside in the area. A few larger unrecognisable prints lead away from the cliffs toward the water. The road runs back west towards the trees, and east to the base of the cliff.

434.name: The Base of the Tordraken Cliffs
434.description: The earth meets the cliffs here. They were cut by the sea rather than by weather, and it shows in the long horizontal scars that mar the rock face from top to bottom, each one a shoreline the water held for a century before it moved on. They rise straight up, never hesitating in their ascent. There are ledges and rims, but none very large, and every one of them is occupied by gulls who resent the intrusion. The cliffs look climbable, but it is not necessary as the road continues to the north up the hill that rests against them. It looks like it is even possible to take a wagon all the way to the top. The road here continues to be well maintained and free of obstruction. To the east, there seems to be a small entrance in the face of the cliff, but it could just be a natural crack.

15760.name: An Uphill Grade On the Path Up the Cliff
15760.description: The road here rises on a pretty steep angle. The side of the cliff is nearby to the east while the hill starts to drop away to the west. The road is smooth and easy to travel aside from the heavy climb. Water cascades cover the large majority of the cliff face here, falling in white ropes from somewhere in the haar above and breaking into spray long before they land. Occasionally the wind takes one sideways and it arrives on the road instead. The road shows signs of passage, though nothing in the way of wear and tear. A few wagon trails are evident in the silt the last rain left, not yet swept away. The climb continues to the north.

15759.name: An Uphill Grade On the Path Up the Cliff
15759.description: The road here rises on a pretty steep angle. The side of the cliff is nearby to the east while the hill starts to drop away to the west. 15761.name: A Bend Around the Great Cascade
15761.description: The road here bends out to the west around a huge fall of water that comes down the side of the cliff out of the cloud like something poured. The column is deep with cold shades of blue and white all through it, and the noise of it fills the whole bend so completely that two people here would have to shout. There are large stones and pieces of rock broken off the cliff lying in the pool at its foot, brought down over the years by the weight of the water. The river the fall feeds is now visible to the south, a shining streak across the bleak landscape running for the sea — an ever present reminder of the powerful nature of this coast, and its total indifference to the plight of man. The road continues to the west.

15762.name: The Path Around the Cascade
15762.description: The road turns into a trail again. It is not quite as permanent as the previous road, almost as if someone keeps moving it westward as the fall widens its pool. It is still manageable however, and there are no major obstructions in the path. The length of the water's reach is now apparent; the spray wets the ground for a few hundred yards. The view of the surrounding countryside to the west is breathtaking. Were it not for the heavy cloud, one could probably see the whole sweep of the Sword Coast from here. The path heads up and to the north.

15763.name: The Path Around the Cascade
15763.description: The road turns into a trail again. It is not quite as permanent as the previous road, almost as if someone keeps moving it westward as the fall widens its pool. It is still manageable however, and there are no major obstructions in the path. The length of the water's reach is now apparent; the spray wets the ground for a few hundred yards. The view of the surrounding countryside to the west is breathtaking. Were it not for the heavy cloud, one could probably see the whole sweep of the Sword Coast from here. The path heads up and to the north.

15764.name: Nearing the Edge of the Cascade
15764.description: The path gets a bit cluttered here. Chunks of fallen rock litter the way as if someone had attempted to roll them back towards the cliff and given up rather quickly. A few gash marks are present in the larger stones, showing that someone did indeed take a blade to the matter, which cannot have helped. Fortunately the hill does not start to drop away for another twenty feet or so to the west, so there is no danger of falling. The approaching drop could be the reason for the attempt. The path heads to the north.

15765.name: Bend In the Path Above the Cascade
15765.description: This is the northern end of the fall, where the water goes over. The path continues east towards the cliff face and south around the pool. The trail starts to look more like a road again here, and the going gets a little easier. The rock at this end is scoured smooth and slick with weed, and the roar comes up from below rather than from beside. The corpse of a huge pack horse lies on the trail. The animal has a visibly broken front leg and bears a massive gash to the neck, presumably a mercy blow. The rain has washed most of the blood away, and what is left has soaked into the stone.

15766.name: The Road Alongside the Cliff Face
15766.description: Wagon tracks are visible here on the road. The trail is now once again a well kept road and no more obstructions bar the way. The cliffs lie directly to the east and the fall to the south and southwest. The going is much easier here, and the shoulder of rock provides some shelter from the wind, which on this coast is worth more than shelter from the rain. The road continues up and to the north.

15767.name: A Steep Rise In the Road Along the Cliff Face
15767.description: The grade continues to rise in angle, making the climb progressively difficult. Neat little piles of swept rock and grit are lined up against the wall; another sign of maintenance. The mineral streak in the rock face becomes more pronounced here, making for a dazzling display when the sun comes through the cloud and finds it. The sheltered vale below no doubt provides a home for a wide variety of creatures, and a wise traveller would be wary. A light grey mist marks the start of the cloud, and foreshadows the top of the cliffs.

15768.name: A Steep Rise In the Road Along the Cliff Face
15768.description: The grade continues to rise in angle, making the climb progressively difficult. Neat little piles of swept rock and grit are lined up against the wall; another sign of maintenance. The mineral streak in the rock face becomes more pronounced here, making for a dazzling display when the sun comes through the cloud and finds it. The sheltered vale below no doubt provides a home for a wide variety of creatures, and a wise traveller would be wary. A light grey mist marks the start of the cloud, and foreshadows the top of the cliffs.

15770.name: The Final Rise To the Top
15770.description: This section of the well kept road leads up and to the north, and appears to be the last stretch before the summit of the Tordraken Cliffs. To the west is almost a straight drop now, as the edge of the hill this road lies on pulls closer. The vale below is no longer visible; it is hidden by a thick cloud cover that is really the sea breathing. The road has begun to take on more uniformity here, and appears to be groomed on a regular basis. The scrub growing out of the cliff face has been cut away and the rock cleaned of weed and salt for several tens of feet off the ground. Leading upward and north, the road continues.

15771.name: Just Beneath the Edge
15771.description: The edge of the cliffs is now completely visible. Just beyond this stretch is the top at long last. Looking back down to the south, it is amazing how fast the road climbs. The cloud is so close it obscures the drop into the vale below, and if one were not aware of the drop it is quite conceivable that one could walk into it. Perfection is the only way to describe the landscaping of the road from here on out. The stones are clean swept, aside from the salt the last blow put down, and the face of the rock is free of weed and scrub. Leading upward and north, the road reaches the summit.

15772.name: The Edge of the Tordraken Cliffs
15772.description: Being so high, this vantage point allows one to see past the cloud directly below. The view is just short of infinite, and beyond fantastic. Mount Gandar looms imperiously to the south, and if it were not for mortal limitations the Calimshan desert would be visible past that. Skeldrach lake shines a deep black in the foreground of Gandar. To the west there is nothing at all but water, going out and out until it stops being a colour. To the north the cliff top runs level and green, cropped short by wind and sheep, except for the castle standing in the middle of it. Leading towards it lies an immaculate road of laid stone. Flags line the sides of the road bearing a device, but they are too far away to make it out.

15774.name: An Immaculate Road Above the Sea
15774.description: The path leading towards the castle is obviously maintained on a daily basis. The stones are swept clear of the salt that comes up the cliff in every blow, and the joints between them have been pointed so recently that some are still pale. The workmanship is comparable to the best dwarven masonry. Flags fly from ashen posts every twenty feet, and on each one, worked in thread that has gone stiff with weather, is the device of Draknor: a dragon's head in profile, jaws closed, on a field of storm grey. The road leads northward towards the castle, and south to the edge of the Tordraken Cliffs.

15775.name: An Immaculate Road Above the Sea
15775.description: The path leading towards the castle is obviously maintained on a daily basis. The stones are swept clear of the salt that comes up the cliff in every blow, and the joints between them have been pointed so recently that some are still pale. The workmanship is comparable to the best dwarven masonry. Flags fly from ashen posts every twenty feet, and on each one, worked in thread that has gone stiff with weather, is the device of Draknor: a dragon's head in profile, jaws closed, on a field of storm grey. The road leads northward towards the castle, and south to the edge of the Tordraken Cliffs.

15776.name: Approaching the Castle
15776.description: It was not clear from the edge of the cliffs exactly how large the castle truly is, as there is nothing on the horizon with which to compare it. The walls are built of a pale translucent stone that takes the light off the water and throws it back, so that on a bright day the whole keep glares like a lantern and on a grey one it looks like a piece of the sky that has set. It is a breathtaking sight and an entirely unwelcoming one: nothing about the frontage suggests a door that opens for strangers. The only comfort it provides is the promise of walls, though one has to wonder whether it might not be safer out here. The road leads northward onto a bridge, and south to the edge of the Tordraken Cliffs.

15777.name: An Arch of Pale Stone Crossing the Cleft
15777.description: The arch is a single span of the same pale stone as the walls, and a deep blue-green light comes up through it from below, pulsing slowly as the swell works in and out. It is perhaps ten feet thick where it meets the ground at either end and, amazingly, no more than a foot at the crown. The stone is always wet and it takes real attention to cross safely. Below the arch the sea has driven a cleft clean through the headland, and the water rushes along it left to right in a horrifying torrent of white and mist, then draws back and does it again. The bottom is not visible. A huge set of double doors can be seen to the north. The immaculate road leads south towards the edge of the cliffs.

15779.name: Before the Doors of Tordraken Castle
15779.description: The majestic double doors bear the dragon's head of Draknor, worn shallow on the seaward side by a century of salt wind, and they are closed with no obvious keyhole. The grand doors open towards the bridge, presumably for security purposes. Giant iron pins form the hinges, connected directly to the iron framework of the door, which in turn is fastened to the stone by smaller shafts driven through the frame and into the wall. Every pin has been greased against the weather and the grease has caught the dust of the road. The stonework is as impressive as the walkway that leads up to it: each stone set on the one below with precision to make sure no ledges are formed which could be used as hand holds. The wall rises perhaps thirty feet into the bleak grey sky. On each of the two visible corners there are towers that rise a few floors above the rest of the castle, and from the parapets of stone all around the top fly banners bearing the same dragon's head.
